label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
Peter—I’m going to disagree with your conclusion, but I want to say first that your diagnosis isn’t wrong. You’ve clearly run payroll and seen the ugly side of advances: the permanent one-month-behind cycle, the recovery problem when someone leaves, the admin drag. I’m not going to pretend those aren’t real. But I think you’re solving for the right risk with the wrong instrument, and we have the scars from trying it your way.

Brenda, I’m writing this mainly for your meeting on the 18th, because you asked for numbers rather than a feeling. Use ours as a template if they help.

We’re about 340 staff, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks, with depots in Embakasi and Changamwe. We closed our advance scheme in February 2025 after exactly the Finance pushback you’re getting. Same argument almost word for word: not a bank, cash flow forecast, people taking advances every month. We gave two months’ notice, did one financial literacy session with the SACCO, and pointed everyone there. It felt responsible. It was a mistake.

In the six months after closure, calls to the office from debt collectors and loan apps went from a handful to **61 logged by reception**. Not 61 in total over the period from one or two people—61 calls that reception actually logged, with names and numbers. Some of the apps were calling supervisors who had been listed as “referees.” That’s the part people miss. The loan is the employee’s private contract until the collection call lands on a supervisor’s phone and the supervisor is trying to do a loading plan while being asked to guarantee someone’s mobile loan.

Unplanned absence on the two days after month-end also rose. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers “sorting out” loans. Three missed runs is not a feeling. It’s a cost, and it doesn’t sit in HR’s budget or Finance’s advance line. It sits in operations, in customer service, in the supervisor’s time, and in the general mess of a depot running short.

And we had one loader at Changamwe who came to me with six apps running at once. He was borrowing from one to pay the other. It took us four months with payroll to unwind it. That is what “the employee’s own decision and their own contract” looks like when it goes wrong. I agree the company shouldn’t be a lender. But when the app calls the office and names a supervisor, the company is already in it. The only question is whether we’re in it with rules or without them.

The SACCO point is the one I’d push back on hardest. SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and need guarantors. That is useless for a child sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. At KES 28,000 a month, there is no emergency buffer. A financial literacy session is useful—we still do them—but it does not create cash on a Tuesday. And the mobile apps, as you say, are the employee’s own decision. Fine. But their collection practices don’t stay private. They call reception, they call supervisors, they call the next of kin. We ended up managing the consequences anyway, just without any ability to cap them.

So we reopened in September 2025, but as a written policy, not the old informal thing. That distinction matters. I don’t defend the old scheme. Someone walking into my office and getting an advance because their supervisor agreed is exactly how you get people taking one every month. The answer to that is rules, not closure.

Our current policy: maximum **40% of net pay**, once per pay cycle, repaid in full at the next payroll, no fee, request through the payroll portal rather than my office. We check the statutory two-thirds limit on total deductions under the Employment Act before approving, so the 40% cap isn’t the only guardrail. Nobody ends up with nothing at month-end. The approval route is payroll/HR, not a line manager’s discretion; the supervisor confirms attendance or operational status, not the amount.

Since reopening we’ve had about **55–70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000**. That’s roughly KES 500,000–630,000 a month, which is a number Finance can forecast. We’ve recovered 100% except for two leavers, with total write-offs of roughly **KES 14,000 for the year**. I’m not saying KES 14,000 is nothing. But compare it with the cost of the 61 calls, the missed runs, the absence, the supervisor time, and the four months spent unwinding one loader’s apps. Those costs are spread across departments, so they never show up in the same place as the advance write-off. That’s why the Finance comparison looks one-sided.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. Not because he’s gone soft, but because the forecast impact is known in advance. It’s a fixed ceiling, not a surprise. He can see the monthly exposure, the recovery rate, and the cap. That’s a very different proposition from an informal scheme where someone can ask for anything.

Peter, you’re right that an informal advance scheme teaches people to live on next month’s money. You’re right that recovery from leavers is a real risk. You’re right that approving advances by hand is a waste of HR time. But the fix for all three is a written policy with a hard cap and a payroll-portal route, not closing the window. Closing the window doesn’t remove the need; it moves it to loan apps at much higher cost, and then the workplace absorbs the collection calls and the absenteeism. We are not a bank—I agree. But a capped advance against wages due at next payroll is not underwriting; it’s payroll timing, with a ceiling.

Brenda, for the 18th, I’d go in with a proposal rather than a defence of the current informal scheme. Something like:

- Written policy, not discretionary.
- Eligibility after probation, and no advance if there’s already one outstanding.
- Cap at 40% of net pay, once per pay cycle.
- Repaid in full at next payroll; no fee, no rollover.
- Request through the payroll portal, approved by payroll/HR, not by walking into your office.
- Check the statutory two-thirds total-deduction limit before approving.
- Monthly report to Finance showing total exposure and recovery, so they can forecast it.
- Review after three or six months with actual numbers: requests, average amount, write-offs, collection calls, absence after month-end.

That gives Finance a ceiling and gives staff a bridge. It also gives you a way to test Peter’s concern honestly: if the data shows people are permanently one month behind, you can tighten frequency or eligibility. But don’t close the window and call it policy. We did that, and the calls started coming to reception.

Peter, if you’ve seen a formal scheme fail—not an informal one, a properly capped and documented one—I’d genuinely like to hear what broke. I’m not trying to win the thread. I’m trying to save Brenda from repeating our six months.
